etymology_ku: Qaşo ji erebî ساعة (sāʕa), hevrreha saet. Nê ber kat (“dem”) dayî, ew gengazkî ji proto-hindûewropî *kʷos, *kʷis e, ku di zimanên din ên hindûewropî da mînakên wê yên wek kengê > dem heye. Guherra dengî wek -k- > -k- di Proto-Hindûîranî da gelek car dibe -ç- > -ç- di Îraniya Navîn da dibe -s- > -sat-; û li gel wî -k- wek xwe dimîne (bide ber çi û kî, ku ji heman bêjeyê hatine dariştin) > -kat-.
Bi pehlewî tarîk, bi îngilîzî dark.

Likely borrowed from Persian آرد (ārd /ârd). See there for more.
Borrowed from Arabic آذَار (ʔāḏār), from Classical Syriac ܐܕܪ (ʾāḏār), ultimately from Akkadian 𒌚𒊺 (addāru).
From Proto-Iranian *Hácmā, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Háćmā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éḱmō. Compare Persian آسمان (âsmân) and Sanskrit अश्मन् (aśman).
From ئاسن (asin, “iron”) + ـگەر (-ger). Compare Persian آهنگر (âhangar).
From Proto-Iranian *HaHcúkah, from *HaHcúš (“fast, quick”) + *-kah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *HaHćúš. Compare Baluchi آسک (ásk) and Persian آهو (âhu).
Compare Old Armenian հաշտ (hašt, “reconciled”), an Iranian borrowing.
A Turkic borrowing, compare Turkish avrat, Azerbaijani arvad. Ultimately from Arabic عَوْرَة (ʕawra).
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meyḱ-. Compare Persian آمیختن (âmixtan).
From Proto-Iranian *Haraθníš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Haratníš (“elbow”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃l- (“to bow; to bend”).

From Proto-Iranian *Hā́fš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hā́ps, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep-. Compare Persian آب (âb), Baluchi آپ (áp), Bakhtiari او (aw), Pashto اوبه, Avestan 𐬀𐬞 (ap), Sanskrit अप् (áp).
From Middle Persian ʾwʾz (āwāč, “voice, sound, tune”).
Variant of هاوزا (hawza), from هاو (haw, “peer, equal”) + زا (za, “born”), from زان (zan, “to give birth”).

From ئاو (aw) + ڕوو (rû). Compare Persian آبرو (âberu).
Compare Persian آیینه (âyine, “mirror”), Baluchi آدینک (ádénk, “mirror”) and Parthian 𐫀𐫀𐫅𐫏𐫗𐫃 (ʾʾdyng /⁠āδēnag⁠/, “mirror”).
Borrowed from Persian آپارتمان (âpârtemân), from French appartement.
ئاژوو (ajû, stem of ئاژوژتن (ajujtin, “to drive”)) + ـەر (-er, agent noun suffix).

Origin uncertain. See Northern Kurdish ala.

Borrowed from Persian آلترناتیو, from French alternative, from Medieval Latin alternativus.

A Turkic borrowing. Compare Turkish iş and Azerbaijani iş.

From Proto-Iranian *jnú, from *ȷ́nú, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ȷ́ā́nu, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu (“knee”). Cognate with Middle Persian [script needed] (šnwk' /⁠šnōg⁠/) and Avestan 𐬲𐬥𐬎 (žnu).

from Proto-Indo-European *éti or Proto-Indo-European *h₁eti. Cognate with Ancient Greek ἔτι (éti), Sanskrit अति (ati), Gothic 𐌹𐌸 (iþ, “and, but, however, yet”), Old English prefix ed- (“re-”). More at ed-.

From Proto-Iranian *bāgáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *bʰāgás. Compare Baluchi باگ (bág) and Persian باغ (bâġ).
From Persian بادام (bâdâm, “almond”). The inherited form is باوی (bawî).

Borrowed from Persian بازار. Doublet of باژاڕ (bajarr), باژێڕ (bajêrr), which were inherited.

etymology_en: From Proto-Iranian *baHjúš (“arm”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *bʰaHȷ́ʰúš, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵʰús. Compare Baluchi باسک (básk), Old Armenian բազուկ (bazuk), Parthian 𐫁𐫀𐫉𐫇𐫃 (bʾzwg /⁠bāzūg⁠/).
Back formation from باشە (başe, “okay, alright, well then”), understood as baş - e ("it is baş", eventually > "it is good"), from Persian باشه. Partially displaced native چاک (çak).
Compare Persian بانو (bânu) and Middle Persian [script needed] (bʾnwk' /⁠bānũg⁠/).

Cognate with Southern Kurdish باوگ (bawg), Northern Kurdish bavik, bav; compare dialectal باو (baw). Ultimately onomatopoeic with a diminutive suffix. This variation with the diminutive was fixed in many Kurdish languages, paired with دایک (dayk).

From Proto-Iranian *wahá-čāra- (“market”) the first and latter elements thereof ultimately deriving from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to sell”) and *kʷel- (“to turn, revolve”) respectively. Cognate with Persian بازار (bâzâr), Gilaki واجار (vājār, “open market, bazaar”), Mazanderani واجار (vājār, “known, reveal”) and Semnani واژار (vāžār).

Borrowed from English Neptune. Ultimately from Latin Neptunus.
From Proto-Iranian *naxusčr̥ya-, from *naxu- (“first, top”) + *sčr̥ya- (“hunting”). Compare Persian نخچیر (naxčīr).
Borrowed from Persian نُرْوِژ, from French Norvège.

etymology_ku: Hevreha belûçî ناسیت (“hilweşandin, binisandin”), ji proto-îranî *nac (“wenda bûn, xuya nebûn”). Ji heman rehî bi pêşgira *wí-: kurmancî binas, binisîn, binisandin, zazakî vindî (“wenda”), farisî گناه (“guneh”).
Hevreha soranî دانەوین (danewîn, “xwe daqûl kirin”), hewramî ئارانامیای (aranamyay, “xwe daqûl kirin”), gişt ji proto-îranî *nam (“çevîn, tewîn”).
Ji proto-îranî *ā- + *bar (“birin, hilgirtin”). Hevreha kurmancî birin û ferwar.
Hevreha peyva xelet, herdu ji erebî غلط (ẍelet). Bo ketina T ji dawiya peyvê, bidin ber "got > go" yan "dît > dî".
Bi rêya farisî هوبره ji erebî حبارى.
Ji هاو (haw, “hev”) + -شار- (rehê dema niha yê شاردنەوە (şardinewe)yê.
Hevreha farisî هو (“kêm, nêm, zox”), îngilîzî sap (“şîrik, şîrav”), ji proto-hindûewropî *sab-, *sap- (“çêjandin, tamandin”).

etymology_en: * From هور (hur, “sun”) + لو (lû, “west”), meaning "sunset, west". The original form was هورلوی (hurlûy, “sunset”), which evolved into modern هەولێر (hewlêr). * From 𒌨𒉈𒈝𒆠 (Urbilum, Urbelum or Urbillum) from Sumerian (Ur) meaning city and (bela) meaning high as the city is located in the upper area, then its meaning corrupted via Akkadian 𒀴𒁀𒉌𒈝 (Arbā'ilu, “four gods”), via Aramaic ܐܪܒܝܠ (Arbel), Ancient Greek Ἄρβηλα (Árbēla), Middle Persian [script needed] (Arbēl). The name entered Kurdish through various historical forms, eventually becoming هەولێر (hewlêr). * From a claimed form meaning "city

etymology_ku: Ji proto-îranî *uxtíš, ji proto-hindûewropî *uktíš (“gotin”). Hevreha kurdiya başûrî وەتن (wetin), hewramî واتەی (watey) (>kurmancî wate), avestayî 𐬎𐬑𐬙𐬌 (ûxtî), ermeniya kevn ուխտ (uxt) (ji zimanekî Îranî), sanskrîtî उक्ति (ûktî). Rayeka dema niha -łê- hewceyî ravekirinê ye.
etymology_en: From Proto-Iranian *uxtíš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *uktíš. Probably unrelated to گوتن (gutin)/کوتن (kutin) or Northern Kurdish gotin. The origin of the present stem -llê- is uncertain.

Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hŕ̥ćšas Proto-Iranian *Hŕ̥šah Central Kurdish ورچ Inherited from Proto-Iranian *Hŕ̥šah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hŕ̥ćšas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos.

From Proto-Iranian *Hhúškah (“dry”), Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hsúškas (“dry”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂sews- (“to be dry”). Cognate with Avestan 𐬵𐬎𐬱𐬐𐬀 (huška, “dry”), Sanskrit शुष्क (śúṣka, “dry”) Persian خشک (xošk, “dry”), Pashto وچ (wəč).
From وشە (wşe, “word”) + نامە (name, “book”), calque of Persian واژهنامه (vâže-nâme).
From the present stem of the verb وەرگێڕان (wergêrran, “to translate”).
Compare Standard Central Kurdish لەگەڵ (legeł), Laki وەگەرد (wagard/vagard), Southern Kurdish وەگەرد (wagard) .
پاراستن (parastin, verb stem پارێز (parêz)) + ـەر (-er, agent noun suffix), literally "one who protects".

etymology_ku: Ji پاسار (pasar, “sivande”) + ـی (-î) ji ber ku beytik bi gelemperî hêlîna xwe li sivandeyan çêdikin. Herwiha bide ber latînî passer (“beytik”).

etymology_en: From Proto-Iranian *pawHākáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *pawHākás, from Proto-Indo-European *pewH-.
From Turkish portakal, from Ottoman Turkish پورتقال (portakal).
From Proto-Iranian *pr̥tuš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *pr̥tuš, from Proto-Indo-European *pértus.

From Proto-Iranian *pr̥sáti, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *pr̥šćáti, from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥sḱéti. Cognate to Persian پرسیدن (porsidan), Sanskrit पृच्छति (pṛcchati), Russian просить (prositʹ), Old English friġnan.
From Proto-Iranian *bišajkah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *bʰišáȷ́. Related to Persian پزشک (pezešk).
Borrowed from Arabic بُولَنْدَا (būlandā), from English Poland.

etymology_ku: Ji paiti (mêr) a avestayî. Hevreha pî (bav) a kirdkî. Hevreha -bat (paşgir; bav) a kurmancî (D) Têkilî peya
etymology_en: Akin to Southern Kurdish پیاگ (pyag), Gurani پیا (pya), Northern Kurdish peya (“pedestrian; man”), from *peyadeg, from *peyad, from Central Kurdish پێ (pê). Compare Persian پیاده.
Compare Classical Persian پیروزه (pērōza, “turquoise”) and Middle Persian *pērōzag.
Compare Middle Persian [script needed] (pys /⁠pēs⁠/, “mottled, leprous; leper”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ-.
From Proto-Iranian *pā́dah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *pā́ts, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds (“foot”).
From Proto-Iranian *pā́dah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *pā́ts, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds (“foot”).
From Proto-Iranian *pā́dah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *pā́ts, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds (“foot”).
پێ (pê, “with, for”) + خەفتن (xef, stem of خەوتن (xewtin, “to sleep”)), literally "for sleeping".
From Proto-Iranian *pánča, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *pánča, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe. Cognate with Northern Kurdish pênc, compare Persian پنج (panj).
From پێ (pê, “with”) + نووسین (nûsîn, “to write”). A purism intended to displace قهڵهم (qellem)

Ultimately from Proto-Iranian *pati- and Proto-Iranian *maH- (“to measure”), the latter from Proto-Indo-Iranian *maH-, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (“to measure”). Cognate with Parthian 𐫛𐫅𐫖𐫀𐫅𐫗 (padmādan, “to measure”), Persian پیمودن (peymudan, “to measure”), Sogdian [script needed] (ptmʾtʾy /⁠patmātē⁠/, “measured, frugal”). Akin to Old Armenian պատմեմ (patmem, “to tell, narrate”), an Iranian borrowing.
From Proto-Iranian *párcuš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *párćuš, from Proto-Indo-European *pérḱus.
Compare Old Armenian պրտու (prtu, “paper reed”), of which the papyrus is made.

etymology_ku: Ji rehê dema niha پەرم- (perm-) (perm-). Bi Proto-Kurdî ve girêdayî ye ku wateya "xwe danîn ser, paldan" dide. Bi kurmancî parastin (piştgirî kirin) re hevreh e.

etymology_en: From Proto-Iranian *pácu, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *páću, from Proto-Indo-European *péḱu.
پەلک (pelk, “arch, branch”) + ـە (e, “connecting vowel”) + زێڕین (zêrrîn, “golden”) + ـە (e, “suffix”)
Compare Northern Kurdish penîr and Persian پنیر (panir).

From Proto-Iranian *parnám, Proto-Indo-Iranian *parnám, From Proto-Indo-European *pornóm, from *p(t)erH. Cognate with Persian پر (par, “feather”), Avestan 𐬞𐬀𐬭𐬆𐬥𐬀 (par^əna, “feather”), Sanskrit पर्ण (parṇá, “feather”), Lithuanian spar̃nas (“wing”), Old Church Slavonic перо (pero, “wing, feather”), Albanian fier (“fern”), English fern.
From Chinese 茶葉 /茶叶 (cháyè, “tea leaves”).
From Proto-Iranian *čaθwā́rah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *čatwā́ras, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
From چا (ça, “tea”) + (the emphatic or definite suffix) ـە (-e).
Compare Persian چراغ (čerâġ) and Parthian 𐫝𐫡𐫀𐫃 (crʾg, “lamp”).
From Proto-Iranian *čaθwā́rah (compare Persian چهار (čahâr)), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *čatwā́ras, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres (compare English four).

From Proto-Indo-European *kyew- (“to move, go”). Cognates include Persian شدن (šodan, “to become , to go”), Ossetian цӕуын (cæwyn), Pashto شول (šwəl), Sanskrit च्यवते (cyávate, “move to and fro, stir”), Old Armenian չու (čʻu) and Ancient Greek σεύω (seúō, “put in quick motion, drive”).
چارە (çare, “face, appearance”) + و (-w) + چاو (çaw, “eye”), from Middle Persian [script needed] (čihrag, “face, appearance”). Cognate with Persian چهره (čehreh, “face”).
From Middle Persian چیون (čiyōn, “as, like, how, when”), from Proto-Iranian *či-gauna.
Literally: “How are you?”, from چۆن (çon, “how”) + ی (î, second person singular copula).
Literally: “How are you? Are you fine?” Compare Persian چطوری خوبی (četori xubi)
A Turkic borrowing. Compare Turkish çökmek (“to kneel”) and Azerbaijani çökmək (“to kneel”). Replaced native ئەژنۆ (ejno) in some dialects.
A Turkic borrowing; compare Turkish çöl, Azerbaijani çöl. Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *čöl (“steppe, desert”).

from Proto-Iranian *čaxrám (compare Avestan 𐬗𐬀𐬑𐬭𐬀 (caxra, “wheel”)), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *čakrám (compare Sanskrit चक्र (cakrá)), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos (“wheel, circle”) (Compare Persian چرخ (čarx)).

From earlier چاشن (çaşn), from [script needed] (çaşnîg, “taste, flavor”), from Parthian [script needed] (çaşnīg, “taste, flavor”) and Middle Persian 𐭰𐭠𐭱𐭭𐭩𐭢 (čašnīg, “taste, flavor”). Related to چێژ (çêj, “pleasure, taste”) and the verb چەشتن (çeştin, “to taste”), cognate with Persian چشیدن (čašidan, “to taste”). Originally meant "taste, flavor" (specifically of food), later extended semantically to mean "type, kind, variety" based on the idea that different things are distinguished by their distinct tastes or qualities when experienced.
From Proto-Indo-European *kʷíh₂onts-, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷíh₂, neuter plural of Proto-Indo-European *kʷís. Compare Persian چند (čand), and Latin quantus.
From Proto-Indo-European *kʷíh₂onts-, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷíh₂, neuter plural of Proto-Indo-European *kʷís. Compare Persian چند (čand), and Latin quantus.
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *selp-. Cognate with Baluchi چرپ (čarp) and Persian چرب (čarb).
A Turkic borrowing. Compare Azerbaijani çapacaq.
Borrowed from Persian رازیانه (râziyâne). Doublet of ڕاژانە (rajane), which was inherited.
From Proto-Iranian *Hraštáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hraštás, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós.
From Proto-Iranian *rā́nah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *srā́nas. Compare Persian ران (rân).
From Arabic رِزْق (rizq, “sustenance, provision”), which is ultimately derived from Middle Persian lwcyk' (rōzīg, “daily bread, sustenance”).

Disputed. Several etymologies have been proposed: # From ڕوبین دژ (rubîn dij, “fortress of polishing”), meaning "fortress of refinement" # From ڕەوان دز (rewan diz, “between two valleys”), shortened from "between two valleys" # From ڕەوەند دز (rewend diz, “fortress of the Rawand tribe”), from the name of the Rawand tribe + دز (diz, “fortress”)
Past participle of روودان (rûdan, “to happen, take place”).
Metathesis of ڕەژوو (reju, “coal”), both being composed of carbon.
From Proto-Iranian *hráwtah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *sráwtas, from Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow”). Compare Persian رود (rôd).
Borrowed from English robot, from Czech robot.
From Proto-Iranian *ráwgnah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ráwgʰnas, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *réwgʰ-no-s (“cream”), from *rewgʰ- + *-nos, from *rew- (“to tear, dig, churn”).
From Proto-Iranian *ráwčah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ráwčas, from Proto-Indo-European *léwk-os ~ *léwk-es-os, from *lewk- (“white, light, bright”). Compare Persian روز (ruz).
From Proto-Iranian *ráwčikah. compare Persian روزی (ruzi) and Parthian [script needed] (rwcyg /⁠rōžīg⁠/).

etymology_ku: Hevreha bextiyarî [skrîpt hewce ye] (rūd, “zarok”), farisî رود (rôd, “zarok”), kumzarî [skrîpt hewce ye] (rōr, “zarok”), gişt ji proto-îranî *frahuHtáh (“zarok”), ji proto-hindûewropî *suH-tós.

etymology_en: From Proto-Iranian *Hráwma, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hráwma. Compare Persian روم (rum).
Compare Northern Kurdish rovî, Avestan 𐬭𐬀𐬊𐬞𐬌 (raopi). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hláwpiš.

etymology_ku: ڕێ (rê, “rê”) + ژوان (jiwan, “jiwan”) (bi soranî anko jivan bi kurmancî)

etymology_en: Borrowed from Persian ژاپُن (žâpon), from French Japon, From Portuguese Japão, from Malay Jepang, from Hokkien 日本 (Ji̍t-pún), from Middle Chinese 日本 (nyit pwon^X, literally “sun origin”).

From Proto-Iranian *hmarati- (“to remember, recall, count”) (possibly with a prefix of unknown origin), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *smárati (“to remember, recollect”). Indo-Iranian cognates include Persian شمردن (“to count”), Pashto شمېرل (śmerël, “to count”), and Sanskrit स्मरति (smárati, “recollect”).
From Proto-Iranian *ǰánHs, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ǰánHs, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn.

From Proto-Iranian *ǰáyHati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ǰáyHati, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷéyh₃eti (“to live”), from the root *gʷeyh₃-. Cognate with Avestan 𐬘𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (juuaⁱti), Persian زیستن, Pashto ژوند کول (žwënd kawël), Sanskrit जीवति (jīvati). More distantly related to Ancient Greek βείομαι (beíomai).
From Proto-Iranian *ǰiHrá- (“lively, vivacious”). Compare Parthian 𐫋𐫏𐫡 (jyr /⁠žīr⁠/, “intelligent, wise”) and Old Armenian ժիր (žir), an Iranian borrowing.
From Proto-Iranian *ǰyáH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ǰyáH, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷyéH.
Compare Persian زنگ (zang), and Armenian ժանգ (žang), an Iranian borrowing.
ژەنین (jenîn, “to play (music)”) + ـیار (-yar, agent suffix), literally "one who plays music".
From Proto-Iranian *ǰaθráH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ǰʰatráH. Compare Persian زهر (zahr) and Old Armenian ժահր (žahr), an Iranian borrowing.
Originally meaning "when", from *kad ~ *ked. Cognate with کەی (key, “when”) which is loaned from Persian کی of the same root. Doublet of سات (sat).
Borrowed from Arabic كَانُون الثَّانِي (kānūn aṯ-ṯānī), from Classical Syriac ܟܢܘܢ ܒ (kānōn b).
Borrowed from Arabic كَانُون الْأَوَّل (kānūn al-ʔawwal), from Classical Syriac ܟܢܘܢ ܐ (kānōn ʾ).
From Proto-Iranian *xāniyaka-, from *xáHh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kʰáHs. Compare Baluchi کانیگ (káníg) and Persian خانی (xâni).

Dara etîmolojiyê Proto-samiya rojavayî *katab- Erebî ك ت ب (k t b) Erebî كِتَاب (kitāb)deyn. Soranî کتێب (kitêb) Soranî -خانە (-xane) Soranî کتێبخانە Ji کتێب (kitêb) + -خانە (-xane).
Dara etîmolojiyê Proto-samiya rojavayî *katab- Erebî ك ت ب (k t b) Erebî كِتَاب (kitāb)deyn. Soranî کتێب (kitêb) Soranî -فرۆش (-froş) Soranî کتێبفرۆش Ji کتێب (kitêb) + -فرۆش (-froş).

etymology_en: From Proto-Iranian *kar-, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kar- (“to do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷer- (“to do, make, construct”).
From Proto-Iranian *kŕ̥miš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kŕ̥miš, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷŕ̥mis (“worm”).
کوتان (kûtan, “to beat, to inoculate”) + ـو (-w, past participle suffix), literally "beaten, inoculated".
کوتان (kûtan, “to beat, to hit”) + ـەک (-ek, diminutive/instrumental suffix), literally "instrument for beating".
From the name in Kurdish, but the exact origins are unclear. See Kurds.
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kuḱis (“(female) pubic hair; vulva”). Compare Persian کس (kos, “vulva”).
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kewh₂-. Cognate with Persian کشتن (koštan).

Proto-Indo-European *kʷo-, the Proto-Indo-European interrogative stem. Cognate with Sanskrit कः (kaḥ, “who, which”), Avestan 𐬐𐬀 (ka, “who”), Hittite 𒆪𒅖 (kuiš, “who”), Latin quī (“who”), Lithuanian kas (“who”), Old Church Slavonic къто (kŭto, “who”), Russian кто (kto, “who”), Old Irish cé (“who”), Welsh pwy (“who”), Old English hwā (“who”).
Compare Old Armenian կոր (kor), Armenian կոռ (koṙ, “curved, crooked”), կռանալ (kṙanal, “to bend over”).

etymology_ku: Herwisan کوندەڵان (kundellan), hevreha farisiya navîn qnd'yh (kundayîh, “cazû, sêr”); ji "kunde" ku navê yeksanî dêwê ku wek "mahîna ku cazûgeran hildigire" tê diyar kirin, + نان (nan, “nan, niyan, danîn”). Hevreha kurmancî kuleşûtik.

etymology_en: From Proto-Iranian *xrináHti, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *krináHti, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷrinéh₂ti.
Compare Persian کلاه (kolâh) and Middle Persian [script needed] (kwlʾp̄ /⁠kulāf⁠/, “cap, bonnet”).
From Proto-Indo-Iranian *kapáwtas (“pigeon”). Cognate with Persian کبوتر (kabutar).

Cognate Classical Persian کَش (kaš, “armpit”).
A Turkic borrowing. Compare Turkish göç and Azerbaijani köç.
A Turkic borrowing, compare Turkish köle, Azerbaijani kölə. Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kȫle.
From Arabic كِيمِيَاء (kīmiyāʔ), from Ancient Greek χῠμείᾱ (khŭmeíā).
From Middle Persian knyc (kanīč, “girl”), from Middle Persian.
From Proto-Iranian [Term?], from Proto-Indo-Iranian, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís.
From Proto-Iranian *kartā-, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Compare Persian کارد (kârd).

Inherited from Proto-Iranian *káršati (“to draw, plough”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *káršati, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷéls-e-ti, from *kʷels- (“to pull, drag”). Cognate with Persian کشیدن, Avestan 𐬐𐬀𐬭𐬱𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (karšaⁱti) and Sanskrit कर्षति (karṣati). Also compare Old Armenian քարշ (kʻarš), an Iranian borrowing.

Borrowed from Arabic كَرْكُوك (karkūk), from Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ܟܲܪܟ݂ܵܐ (karḵā), from Aramaic כַּרְכָא (karḵā), from either Demotic Egyptian grg or from the root ܟ ܪ ܟ (k r k) related to encircling.
Borrowed from Persian, ultimately from Ancient Greek κράμβη (krámbē).

From Proto-Iranian *kanyáH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kanyáH, from Proto-Indo-European *ken-. Compare Baluchi کنشک (kinišk), Persian کنیزک (kanizak) and Parthian 𐫑𐫗𐫏𐫝𐫃 (qnycg /⁠kanīžag⁠/). Doublet of کچ (kiç) and کەنی (kenî).
Akin to Persian خندیدن (xandidan, “to laugh”). See it for more.
Compare Persian کبک (kabk) and Middle Persian [script needed] (kpk' /⁠kabk⁠/, “partridge”).
From Proto-Iranian *kamān (“arc, vault, bow”). Compare Persian کمان (kamân).
Compare Persian کفچه (kafče) and Middle Persian [script needed] (kpck' /⁠kafčag⁠/, “spoon, ladle”).
From Proto-Iranian *gā́wš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *gā́wš, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (“cattle”).
From earlier گائاسن (ga'asin). Equivalent to گا (ga, “bull, ox”) + ئاسن (asin, “iron”).
Compare Classical Persian گرفتن (giriftan). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebh₂- (“to grab, seize”).
From Proto-Iranian *gr̥Híš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *gr̥Híš, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH-.
From Proto-Iranian *gáwbati, from Proto-Indo-European *gewH- (“to call, cry”) with a *-b⁽ʰ⁾- enlargement, perhaps connected to the synonymous *ǵʰewH-. Cognate with Persian گفتن (goftan, “speak”).
From Proto-Iranian *wŕ̥kah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian * wŕ̥kas, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos.
Compare Persian گند (gond, “testicle”) and Middle Persian [script needed] (gwnd /⁠gund⁠/).
Compare Persian گوز (gowz) and Old Armenian ընկոյզ (ənkoyz), an Iranian borrowing.

etymology_en: From Middle Persian [script needed] (gwšk' /⁠gōšag⁠/, “corner”), which appears to be a suffixed formation from the word found now as گوش (guš, “ear”), in the sense of a lappet or protruding end of something.
The original form is گێسک (gêsk), from earlier *wēsk, ultimately from Proto-Iranian *wacyakah.
From Proto-Iranian *garmáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *gʰarmás, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰor-mó-s. Cognate with Persian گرم (garm) and English warm.
According to Henbane Borîne, the name means "lively, fresh and energetic".
A Turkic borrowing, compare Turkish gemi, Azerbaijani gəmi. Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kēmi, *gẹ̄mi (“boat”).

Two possible etymologies: # From Proto-Germanic *gamaną (“joy, pleasure, amusement”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰem- (“to rejoice”). Related to Old English gamen (“game, sport”), German Gammeln (“merriment”). # From گام (gam, “step”), referring to the movements or steps involved in play and games.

From Arabic قَوَّاد (qawwād). Taken from a Mesopotamian Arabic dialect, hence /g/ instead of /q/.
From Classical Syriac ܓܒܪܐ (gaḇrā), from Aramaic 𐡂𐡁𐡓𐡀 (gbrʾ /⁠gaḇrā⁠/, “man; person”)
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *semh₂- (“year”). Compare English summer.
From Proto-Iranian *hájah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *sáȷ́ʰas, from Proto-Indo-European *séǵʰos.
From Proto-Iranian *Háydma, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Háydʰma, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“to burn; fire”). Compare Persian هیزم (hizom) and Talysh ایزم (izəm).

From Proto-Iranian *náyHatī, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *náyHati (“to lead”), from Proto-Indo-European *néyHeti, derived from the root *neyH- (“to lead”).

Compare Classical Persian امرود (amrōd, “pear”), Middle Persian [Book Pahlavi needed] (ʾwlmwt' /⁠urmōd⁠/, “pear”), Old Persian [script needed] (*umrūta).

From Proto-Iranian *hajáhram, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *saȷ́ʰásram, from Proto-Indo-European *sm̥-ǵʰéslom. Indo-Iranian cognates include Northern Kurdish hezar, Baluchi ہزار (hazár), Persian هزار (hazâr), Pashto زر (zër), Ossetian ӕрзӕ (ærzæ), and Sanskrit सहस्र (sahásra). Non-Indo-Iranian cognates include Latin mille and Ancient Greek χίλιοι (khílioi). Akin to Old Armenian հազար (hazar), a Middle Iranian borrowing.

Compare Classical Persian افسان (afsān), فسان (fasân), سان (sân, “whetstone”). Ultimately from Proto-Iranian *abi-saH-na- or *ham-saH-na-, from Proto-Iranian *saH- (“to whet, cut”). Compare also Armenian հեսան (hesan), from Old Armenian յեսան (yesan), which formerly was considered as the source of the Kurdish word.
Cognate with Northern Kurdish heşt, from Proto-Iranian *aštā́, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *aštā́, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Compare Persian هشت (hašt).
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sm-o-. Compare Persian همه (hame).
From Proto-Iranian *Hangubáynah, from *Hángwr̥ (“extract, resin”) + *báynah (“bee”). Cognate with Persian انگبین (angobin, angabin) and Talysh انگوین (anqevin).

From Proto-Iranian *abráh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *abʰrás, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥bʰrós (“rain-cloud, rain, cloud”). Cognates include Avestan 𐬀𐬡𐬭𐬀 (aβra), Sanskrit अभ्र (abhrá), Old Armenian ամբ (amb), Latin imber and Ancient Greek ἀφρός (aphrós).
From Proto-Iranian *hampr̥sā. Cognate with Persian ارس (ors)/اورس (avers), Baluchi اپرس (apors, “juniper”).
From earlier *Eblêr with h-extension, from *Erbêl. compare Middle Persian [script needed] (Arbēl).
From Proto-Iranian *hapáθniH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *sapátniH, from *sa- (“together, co-”) + *pátniH (“wife”), from Proto-Indo-European *pótnih₂ (“wife”).
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sers- (“to cut off”). Compare Latin serra (“saw”), Persian اره (arre, “saw”), Mazanderani هره (hare, “saw”), and Baluchi ہرگ (harrag, “saw”).
Equivalent to ھەشت (heşt, “eight”) + دە (de, “ten”). Compare Persian هجده (hejdah).
From Proto-Iranian *Hr̥jifyáh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hr̥ȷ́ipyás, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂rǵ-i-pt-ió-s, from *h₂erǵ- (“white, glittering”).

etymology_ku: Ji tirkî yaka. یەخە (yexe) ya soranî, یقه (yeqê) û یخه (yexê) yên farisî û ياقة (yaqe) ya erebî hemû ji yaka ya tirkî ne ku hevreha yakın (“nêzîk”) û yaklaşmak (“nêzîk bûn”) in ku ji *jaka ya tirkiya kevn e û hevreha wê wek cakag di mongolî de jî peyda dibe.

etymology_en: From Proto-Iranian *Háywakah, derivative of Proto-Iranian *Háywah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Háywas. Related to Persian یک (yek).
